blocks.text: J. D. Michaelis, in Supplemm. ad Lexx. Hebrr. vol. 2, p. 388, holds that the name דבורה was given to bees from pursuing, since scarcely any other animal is fiercer in pursuit. This etymology would be apt enough, if only the verb דבר meant to pursue. For Michaelis takes the Piel conjugation of that verb in this sense at 2 Paral, XXII, 10, and renders the whole passage ותדבר את כל זרע הממלכה thus: she pursued, namely to destruction, all the royal seed. This seems to be rejected if only because the verb nowhere else in the O. T. occurs in that sense, nor does that notion suit any passage; [III, 353] not to mention that in none of the languages cognate with Hebrew is this verb used in that sense. The etymology proposed by Bochart is therefore preferable, and Storr also approved it in Observatt. ad Anal. et Syntax. Hebr. p. 5, note. Michaelis rightly observes, however, that the Syriac ܕܒܘܪܐ is a somewhat broader name than the Hebrew, also covering wasps and hornets, and is used for the Hebrew צרעה at Exod. XXIII, 28. Deut. VII, 20. Ios. XXIV, 12.

Compare what has been collected from other writers on the birth of bees from an ox by Schoettgen on Varro 2, 5, 5; Alberti on Hesychius, under the word Βουγενέων [bougeneōn]; van Goens on Porphyry, Antr. Nymph. p. 104; and Niclas on the Geopon. book 15, ch. 2, §§ 14, 24, p. 1064 and 1070.

It does not, however, seem necessary to understand ימים in the story of Samson as the space of a year, since in those regions the heat of the sun so dries out carcasses within a few days that only the framework of the bones, covered with hide, remains, as Oedmann rightly observes in Vermischten Sammlungen, part 6, Chapter 20, p. 135 f., German trans.

Nor has anyone yet been able to find organs of hearing in bees. Oedmann, loc. cit., therefore thinks that the Hebrew poet at Es. V, 26. and VII, 18. means only this in general: that the countless armies of Assyria would be ready at a nod to inflict on the Israelites the punishments announced by Jehovah.

Rather: with dung, as Palladius also has it (who follows Columella so closely that he seems to have compiled his writings), De re rustica, book 7, ch. 7, § 2: smoke is applied from galbanum and dry cow dung. Didymus in the Geoponica, book 15, Chapter 4, § 6: Ἠρινῶν δε δεκα ἡμερων διελθουσων, καπνῳ βολβιτου ξηρου ἐπι τας νομας αὐτας ἐξελασας, καθαρισεις και κορησεις τα ἀγγεια [Ērinōn de deka hēmerōn dielthousōn, kapnō bolbitou xērou epi tas nomas autas exelasas, kathariseis kai korēseis ta angeia]. But after ten days of spring have passed, you will drive them out to pasture with the smoke of dry cow dung, and you will clean and sweep the vessels. The same, Chapter 5, § 5: Χρη δε καπνῳ βολβιτου προαπολαυνειν αὐτας [Chrē de kapnō bolbitou proapolaunein autas].
